newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE-Gas vehicles set for big growth in Britain.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Gas vehicles set for big growth in Britain.

text.p: A tax break in Britain's November budget aimed at promoting natural gas as an alternative to petrol and diesel has prompted predictions that fleets of gas vehicles could be running on city streets in a few years.
"Within about five years we would expect about 200,000 compressed natural gas (CNG) vehicles on the road," said Fred Parker, executive director of the Natural Gas Vehicle Association (NGVA).
"Most will be urban commercial vehicles - and this will be quite a reasonable proportion, about five percent, of all the four million commercial vehicles in Britain."
The NGVA, which brings together about 50 companies involved in vehicle manufacturing and related areas, has seen a threefold rise in enquiries since the budget, most from local authorities.
In the budget, Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke cut duty on road fuel gases by 25 percent, following a 15 percent cut the year before.
Before that the National Air Quality Strategy, which sets out targets on air quality to be introduced by 2005, had already put the onus on local authorities to improve air quality.
Gas is attractive because it is a cleaner burning fuel than petrol or diesel. It does not produce particulates to pollute the atmosphere.

Tom Gorman, head of British Gas Natural Gas Vehicles said the budget move cut the pump price to around 44 pence a litre of gasoline equivalent, down from 48.5 pence a litre previously. Duty on petrol and diesel was raised by three pence a litre.
But Britain has a long way to go before it can compete internationally in the gas vehicle market.
Parker said there were only around 450 gas-fuelled vehicles on the road in Britain, compared with 300,000 in Italy and possibly as many as 500,000 in Russia.
"Most vehicles are car-derived, for example delivery vans, although they go all the way through to 32.5 tonne trucks, and there's also a smattering of private cars," he said.
The bus market is also opening up.
"Southampton's Citybus invested in 16 buses last year. That may not sound like many, but there are only between 3,000 and 3,500 new buses sold in Britain every year," said Parker.
Volvo recently sold 14 gas powered buses to an urban bus company in central England.
"That's where the market will develop, with buses and delivery vehicles in urban areas. That's the best case for environmental improvement, as these vehicles are replacing diesel, not petrol."
In central London, 20 percent of air pollution comes from diesel-fuelled buses and taxis.

Given continued government support, Parker expects the market to grow, with the first wave of interest coming from fleet operations where the vehicle returns to a home base during the day -- as buses do on fixed routes.
"We would expect that after four or five years of growth, we will see the development of refuelling facilities in service stations alongside petrol and diesel."

Once the 200,000 vehicle mark has been reached, Parker expects to see dedicated vehicles produced, instead of conversions from petrol or diesel. This will bring costs down, and refuelling facilities should also become more widely available.
But a refuelling development in Ontario, Canada, may also make CNG vehicles more attractive for the private market.
In Ontario about 2,000 homes are fitted with compressors attached to existing gas lines delivering gas for domestic use, allowing drivers to fill up with natural gas at home.
The refuelling lines have to be separately metered, allowing excise duty to be levied, but Parker says the method is being heavily promoted.

"Although CNG vehicles are much more widely used in Italy and Russia than in Britain, they were developed there through fiscal incentives and because of the availability of gas, not from environmental considerations", Parker said.
"So technology in Britain is generally superior, as it was developed from an environmental viewpoint, not just from conversion of existing vehicles."
Executives from the giant oil companies are more guarded.

John Browne, group chief executive of British Petroleum said last month that natural gas has the potential to become next century's "fuel of choice" in Europe, although he doubted that it would become an important transport fuel.
Henk Dijkgraaf, chief executive, gas and coal at Royal Dutch/Shell echoed that view. "Gas will probably not replace oil products for transportation purposes in our lifetime," he said early this year.
